newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Publishers demand changes to copyright law.
newsitem.headline: Publishers demand changes to copyright law.

text.p: Europe's publishing industry on Tuesday urged in-depth changes to European copyright law to ensure that companies rather then journalists hold the rights to their works in the information society.

"The major concern is that in many European countries, copyright is still vested in the individual creator irrespective of whether the work is created under a regular employment contract or who bears the financial risk," the European Publishers Council said in a statement.
Sir Frank Rogers, Chairman of the Council, said that the publishing industry might have a social cultural, and political role, but it was none of these if it could not work as a business.
"None of us can perform any of these functions unless we are economically viable," he told a news conference.

Kerstin Rinne, Vice-President of Sanoma Corporation in Finland, said the European Union's work on copyright in the developing information society had so far concentrated on the means of patrolling copyright, rather than the copyright concepts themselves.
The publishers say the current approach leaves them ill-equipped to compete with other media players and competitors from outside the European Union.

"When copyrights are vested in the employees we, as publishers, face costly copyright clearance processes and multiple payments, restricted availability and use of old material...before all economic risks are taken," it said.
"Many European publishers are thereforce discouraged from investing in new products and services, faced with the need to secure rights for everyday business development."
The EPC and other publishing groups said the EU should take over the system used in the United States, Britain and the Netherlands, where the employer holds the copyright.
